turns.prompt_text: When extracting honey from a b frame the traditional way is to use centrifugal force force the honey out I imagine there are better ways now days
turns.response_html:
The classic radial or tangential centrifuge extractor is still the commercial standard because it's highly efficient at scale, but you are spot on—the honey harvesting landscape has changed quite a bit. Modern alternatives focus on eliminating the heavy, expensive spinner, reducing mess, or preventing the need to destroy or alter the wax comb.

Here is how the modern approach breaks down, ranging from automated hive designs to low-tech, small-scale extraction.

1. Flow Hives (Extraction In-Situ)

The biggest shift in backyard beekeeping over the last decade is the Flow Hive system. Instead of removing the frame, uncapping the wax, and spinning it, the extraction happens right inside the hive while the bees are completely undisturbed.

  • How it works: The frames use a food-grade plastic matrix that forms incomplete honeycomb cells. The bees seal the cells with their own natural wax and fill them with honey. When it's time to harvest, you insert a metallic key and turn it 90 degrees.
  • The Mechanism: The split-cell design shifts vertically, creating a zig-zag channel inside the comb. Gravity allows the honey to flow straight down to a sealed trough at the bottom of the frame and out into your jars via a rear tube. Turning the key back resets the cells for the bees to reuse.

2. Unassisted Gravity Drainage (Crush and Strain)

If you are looking for a low-cost alternative to a centrifuge that doesn't involve buying expensive specialized hive systems, the Crush and Strain method is the go-to alternative for small-scale apiaries.

  • How it works: You pull the honeycomb entirely off the frame wedge top-bars or cut the comb out of foundationless frames. The wax and honey are thoroughly crushed together in a sterile bucket using a heavy-duty potato masher or clean hands.
  • The Separation: The mixture is poured through a tiered mesh straining system (typically a 600-micron coarse filter followed by a 400 or 200-micron fine filter). Gravity does 100% of the work over 12–24 hours, separating crystal-clear honey from the wax cap material.
  • The Trade-off: The bees have to completely rebuild the comb from scratch next season, which consumes significant colony energy (roughly 6–8 lbs of honey consumed per pound of wax produced). However, it yields an incredible amount of clean, premium rendering wax.

3. Commercial Vacuum Extraction (Experimental / Industrial)

On the high-tech, commercial industrial end, some operations are shifting away from high-RPM centrifugal spinners toward low-pressure vacuum extraction manifolds.

  • How it works: The frames are uncapped mechanically via hot knives or rollers, then placed into an airtight chamber. Instead of spinning the frames rapidly (which can fracture brittle, cold wax foundation or blowout frames), a controlled vacuum environment drops the ambient pressure.
  • The Benefit: The pressure differential pulls the honey uniformly out of the cells from both sides simultaneously. It reduces mechanical stress on the wooden frames, completely eliminates the high vibration and noise of large spinners, and handles high-viscosity honeys (like heather or manuka honey) much better than standard force.

Another thought comes to mind. Why don't they just heat the entire frames up until everything melts off? And then separate the beeswax from the honey later? Assuming you cannot melt the honey alone without getting all the wax as well
turns.response_html:
The reason we don't just melt the whole frame down to separate them later comes down to a fundamental thermal limitation of honey: honey degrades permanently at temperatures far below the melting point of beeswax.

If you crank up the heat enough to liquefy the comb, you accidentally ruin the quality, flavor, and legal definition of the honey long before the wax ever melts.

Here is exactly why this thermal approach breaks down:

1. The Thermal Mismatch

To melt everything off the frame, you have to hit the melting point of the substance with the higher threshold.

  • Beeswax Melting Point: Clean beeswax melts at roughly 143°F to 147°F (62°C to 64°C).
  • Honey Damage Threshold: Honey begins to suffer severe thermal degradation, loss of volatile aromatic compounds, and destruction of beneficial enzymes at anything above 104°F to 113°F (40°C to 45°C).

To melt the wax completely, you have to overshoot the honey's safety limit by more than 30°F.

2. Chemical Changes: HMF and Pasteurization

When honey is subjected to the ~145°F temperatures required to liquefy beeswax, two major chemical changes occur:

  • Caramelization and HMF Spikes: The complex natural sugars (fructose and glucose) begin to break down and scorch. This causes a rapid rise in Hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF), a chemical byproduct of sugar decomposition. High HMF levels turn the honey dark, introduce a bitter, burnt-sugar flavor, and legally disqualify it from being sold as raw or high-grade honey.
  • Enzyme Denaturation: Raw honey is prized for live enzymes like diastase, invertase, and glucose oxidase (which gives honey its natural antimicrobial properties). Sustained heat completely denatures these proteins, essentially turning a live, complex whole food into a dead, simple sugar syrup.

3. The Nightmare of Post-Separation

Even if you didn't care about cooking the honey, separating them post-melt is incredibly messy.

When wax melts, it doesn't just sit on top neatly right away; tiny colloidal micro-particles of wax, propolis, and larval cocoons become suspended throughout the hot, viscous honey. Trying to filter molten wax out of hot honey requires ultra-fine filtration that frequently clogs, and any microscopic wax particles left behind will cool, solidify, and leave a gritty, waxy film on the roof of your mouth when you eat it.

Alternative: The Solar Wax Extractor

Beekeepers do actually use heat to separate honey and wax, but only for the leftover waste scrapings (called "cappings") after the main harvest is already done. They use a Solar Wax Extractor—an insulated box with a glass top.

The sun heats the interior just enough to melt the cappings. The molten wax and residual honey drip down into a sloped pan. Because wax is lighter than honey, it floats to the top and solidifies into a clean cake as it cools, leaving a layer of dark, cooked honey underneath. Beekeepers call this "baker's honey"—it's no longer good for table use because it tastes scorched, but it works fine for industrial baking where it's going to be cooked anyway!
